Caring Village: A shared family app with a calendar, to-dos, medication lists, documents and an AI helper.
Built by former caregivers as one place for the whole family's care.
Shared calendar and medication list keep all siblings on the same care information.
Loses entries, resets the care plan, shows medical details to friends, and cannot get relatives to join.
The caregiver pays: free for 2 people, or $14.99 to $24.99 a month.
Partly: an AI helper answers care questions. No help with dementia behavior.
Partly: less stress and back-and-forth. Takes no care tasks off the caregiver.
Partly: stores documents. No help getting into bank, insurer or portal accounts.
No: nothing for a parent who refuses help.
Partly: relatives join free with their own login. Can't make them do tasks.
Everplans: Online vault for documents, accounts and wishes, shared with chosen family.
Walks a person through organizing all their life details and next steps.
Gives adult children the parent's accounts, insurance policies and end-of-life wishes in one place.
Useless unless the parent filled it in. The iPad app runs only at phone size.
The parent pays: free for 3 items, or $99.99 a year.
No: stores papers only. No care or behavior advice.
No: takes no care work or time off the caregiver.
Yes, if the parent fills it in: accounts, papers, insurance and wishes in one vault.
No: the parent must fill it in and can lock sections until death.
Partly: relatives see chosen sections. Nothing splits the work.
Cariloop: A personal care coach, a care-booking marketplace, a family Care Team and document storage.
Full-time coaches who take no money from the care providers they suggest.
Assigns a full-time care coach who guides families through a crisis.
Available only through employers with 100 or more workers. The app freezes.
The employer pays. At MSU, keeping the coach yourself costs $249 a month.
Yes: coaches explain diagnoses like Alzheimer's and find the right doctors and care.
Partly: coaches find and book care. Only if the employer offers it.
Yes: help paying for care, with Medicare, Medicaid and VA benefits, and POAs.
Partly: coaches handle family dynamics. Nothing for a parent who refuses.
Partly: relatives join the Care Team and get updates. Tasks aren't split.
A Place for Mom: A free advisor, a care and cost check, local places with prices, and tours.
Says it has the country's largest senior care network.
Lists nearby senior living options with prices and books tours.
Shares families' contact details, causing nonstop sales calls. Commission-paid advisors know little about the places.
Senior living places pay it when a family moves in. Free to families.
Partly: an advisor guides the search. Advisors often don't know the places.
Partly: saves search time. Nonstop calls add stress.
Partly: cost calculator and assessment. No help for Medicaid-only families.
No: an advisor told one family to lie to the parent to move her.
No: one family contact. Nothing for relatives to share.
Geriatric care managers: None of the 14 segments (private care management)
Home visits, care plans, hiring and checking aides, appointments, and help for families far away.
Trained local professionals who see the parent and the home in person.
Attend doctor visits, evaluate care facilities and arrange respite during a crisis.
Cost $150 to $300 an hour, offer unclear services, and sometimes never make the agreed care plan.
The family pays $150 to $300 an hour. Medicare and Medicaid usually don't.
Yes: explain hard topics to the parent and family, and make a care plan.
Yes, for a price: respite, doctor visits and place tours taken off the caregiver.
Partly: advise on financial options. One took power of attorney without telling the family.
Partly: talk with the parent directly. Some parents still refuse them.
Partly: stand up to difficult relatives. Family fights often follow.
Group texts and notebooks: What families use instead (not a company)
Family group chats, notebooks, binders and whiteboards.
Everyone already has them, they're free, and there's nothing to install.
Reach every relative instantly for free. A whiteboard schedule reduces a parent's repeated questions.
Help requests get ignored or just a 'like.' Notes and calendars get lost or erased.
Nobody: they're free or nearly free.
Partly: a written guide lets someone else step in. No advice on what to do.
No: constant messages wear the caregiver down.
Partly: a binder holds papers. Records pile up and can't be searched.
Partly: work without the parent using any tech. Nothing helps when the parent refuses.
Partly: everyone hears at once. Requests get silence or a 'like'.
Area Agencies on Aging: None of the 14 segments (free public service)
Caregiver information, help finding services, counseling, support groups, training and respite.
Local, government-funded and free to families who qualify.
Connect families to free local services, support groups and Medicare counseling. Some fund respite.
Mostly referrals, long waitlists, hard-to-reach staff and strict eligibility.
Federal and state grants pay. Free to families who qualify.
Partly: information and training. Staff often don't know the answer.
Partly: can pay for respite or home help. Long waits and strict rules.
Partly: Medicare counseling. Otherwise referrals, no hands-on help with accounts.
No: can't act without the parent's consent.
No: services go to one caregiver. Nothing for relatives to share.
